The encoding of MAM for Sefaria

Author: Ben Denckla

Revision: 2026-10-26

Introduction

MAM (Miqra According to the Masorah) is a digital edition of the Hebrew Bible, based on the Aleppo Codex and related manuscripts, whose text is on Hebrew Wikisource. MAM-for-Sefaria is the extract of MAM that Sefaria imports and shows as its default Tanakh. This page describes what the files of MAM-for-Sefaria have, and how they encode it.

The files are in the MAM-for-Sefaria directory of the repository MAM-basics, whose README says how current they are. Every count, and every example of MAM-for-Sefaria, on this page is taken from those files.

This page has three typographic conventions:

  1. Text styled like this reveals more on hover, where the medium allows hovering.
  2. Text styled like this draws attention to letters of a form, as to the ב of אבג.
  3. ZARQA is the name of a Unicode code point, less the words that name its script and class. Hovering shows the whole name, here HEBREW ACCENT ZARQA.

The files

MAM-for-Sefaria has four folders. Each has one file for each of the 39 books, named by the book's title on Sefaria, as I Samuel.csv is, and a provenance note, _provenance.md.

Folder Verse numbering Verses What a file has
csv/ Sefaria's 23,206 each verse's reference and its text in HTML, after five header rows
csv-ajf/ BHS's 23,213 each verse's reference and plain text, and its two strands where it has two cantillations
misc/unicode-names/ Sefaria's 23,206 the code points of each verse of csv/
misc/unicode-names-ajf/ BHS's 23,213 the code points of each verse of csv-ajf/

The csv/ folder

Each file of csv/ is a CSV file in UTF-8, with CRLF line ends and no byte-order mark. Its first five rows are a header, each row a key and its value. Every file has the same values, but for the first:

Key Value
Index Title the book's title on Sefaria
Version Title Miqra according to the Masorah
Language he
Version Source https://he.wikisource.org/wiki/%D7%9E%D7%A7%D7%A8%D7%90_%D7%A2%D7%9C_%D7%A4%D7%99_%D7%94%D7%9E%D7%A1%D7%95%D7%A8%D7%94
Version Notes the paragraph of HTML below

The value of Version Notes, rendered, is:

Miqra According to the Masorah (MAM) is a digital Hebrew edition of the Tanakh based on the Aleppo Codex and related manuscripts. It is designed for readers, and as such it contains added elements to aid vocalization of the text. For instance: When an accent is marked in an unstressed syllable, an extra accent is added in the proper place (pashta, zarqa, segol, telisha). Legarmeih and paseq are visibly distinguished. Qamaz qatan is indicated by its designated Unicode character (alternatives are documented where traditions differ about its application).
The text of MAM is fully documented. The complete introduction to the edition (Hebrew) explains the types of editorial decisions that have been made and the reasons for them (English abstract). In addition, every word in the Bible about which there is some textual concern or ambiguity includes a documentation note; these notes can be viewed conveniently here. If an error is discovered, it may be reported to User:Dovi at Hebrew Wikisource. Please check the documentation notes before reporting an error.

After the header, each of the 23,206 rows is a verse, with two fields: the verse's reference, such as Genesis 1:1, and the verse's text, in HTML.

The csv-ajf/ folder

The files of csv-ajf/ are the AJF variant. They are CSV files in UTF-8 with CRLF line ends, as those of csv/ are, but they have no header, and their verses are numbered as in BHS. Each of their 23,213 rows has four fields: the verse's reference, its text, and its cant-alef and cant-bet strands, which are empty but in the 24 verses that have two cantillations: Genesis 35:22; Exodus 20:2–6, 20:8–10 and 20:13–15; and Deuteronomy 5:6–10, 5:12–15 and 5:17–19.

In those verses the second field has the text that represents both strands, as csv/ has it too. The third and fourth fields have the strands themselves, which are, as the guide to MAM-simple's JSON says, the תחתון and עליון strands in the Decalogues, and the פשוטה and מדרשית strands at Genesis 35:22.

Their text is plain: it has no HTML, and neither of the two spaces that csv/ writes as character references. So they spell some things differently:

csv/ csv-ajf/
a samekh break NO-BREAK SPACE, then {ס} in a span, then eight more SPACE, {ס}, SPACE
a pe break NO-BREAK SPACE, then {פ} in a span, then <br> SPACE, {פ}, SPACE
a legarmeh THIN SPACE, then PASEQ in <b> PASEQ, right after its atom
a paseq THIN SPACE, PASEQ in <small>, THIN SPACE two PASEQ marks, with no space on either side
a space of song spacing eight NO-BREAK SPACE characters SPACE
a ketiv and its qere in the order MAM has them the ketiv first
a trivial pair, an implicit maqaf, or a small, large or hung letter in a span or element of its own the text alone

In the text field of csv-ajf/, each of these has the count it has in csv/: 1,787 legarmeh and 508 paseq marks, 1,982 samekh and 1,571 pe breaks, and 1,047 pairs of a ketiv and its qere.

The Unicode-name listings

Each file of misc/unicode-names/ lists the code points of one book of csv/, and each file of misc/unicode-names-ajf/ those of one book of csv-ajf/. They are text files in UTF-8, with LF line ends. A listing's first line is unicode_names Genesis, for its book. Then each verse has a line that names it, a line for each run of its text, and a blank line, but for the last verse.

The line that names a verse has the book's identifier in MAM-basics, the chapter and verse, and the verse numbering, as Genesis 1:5 in vtrad vtsef and Levit 1:1 in vtrad vtbhs do. Each SPACE and NO-BREAK SPACE has a line of its own, with its name, and so splits the text into runs. A run's line has its code points, separated by commas, each by the short name that the table below gives it. In misc/unicode-names/, each HTML element has lines of its own: one with START and the element's tag and class before its contents, and one with STOP after them, or a single line with START/STOP for br, which has no contents. In misc/unicode-names-ajf/, a verse with two cantillations lists each of its three texts after a line that names it, rv-cant-combined, rv-cant-alef or rv-cant-bet, with the text's lines indented by four spaces.

For example, Genesis 1:5 has this text in csv/:

וַיִּקְרָ֨א אֱלֹהִ֤ים ׀ לָאוֹר֙ י֔וֹם וְלַחֹ֖שֶׁךְ קָ֣רָא לָ֑יְלָה וַֽיְהִי־עֶ֥רֶב וַֽיְהִי־בֹ֖קֶר י֥וֹם אֶחָֽד׃ {פ}

Verse numbering

The verses of csv/ are numbered as Sefaria numbers them, and those of csv-ajf/ as BHS numbers them, so a reference can name different text in the two folders. The page Versification Differences: MAM, BHS, and Sefaria lists the differences. Every reference of csv/ is also in csv-ajf/, which has 7 more: Exodus 20:24–26, Numbers 25:19 and Deuteronomy 5:31–33.

Both numberings have Joshua 21:36–37, for which MAM has no text. In both folders, each of these rows has only an EM DASH (—), since an empty field would let the text of another version show at that verse on Sefaria. The files have no other EM DASH.

Markup

The verse text of csv/ is HTML with 6 elements, of which only span has an attribute, its class. These are all the elements and classes that the files have:

Element Class Count What it holds
span mam-spi-samekh 1,982 a samekh break, {ס}
span mam-spi-pe 1,571 a pe break, {פ}
span mam-spi-invnun 9 an inverted nun, NUN HAFUKHA
span mam-implicit-maqaf 116 a gray maqaf (see Gray maqaf)
span mam-kq 1,047 a ketiv and its qere
span mam-kq-k 1,055 a ketiv, in parentheses
span mam-kq-q 1,056 a qere, in square brackets
span mam-kq-trivial 149 a trivial ketiv/qere pair, as one pointed atom
span k-velo-q-maq 2 a maqaf after a ketiv velo qere
b 1,787 the PASEQ of a legarmeh
small 531 the PASEQ of a paseq (508), or a small letter (23)
big 27 a large letter
sup 4 a hung letter
br 1,571 nothing: it follows each pe break

Legarmeh and paseq

A legarmeh and a paseq are both the code point PASEQ. The files tell them apart by markup and spacing:

Example Reference Mark Encoding Count
וְכֹ֣ל ׀ שִׂ֣יחַ Genesis 2:5 legarmeh THIN SPACE, then PASEQ in <b>, then the space before the next atom 1,787
אֱלֹהִ֤ים ׀ לָאוֹר֙ Genesis 1:5 paseq THIN SPACE, PASEQ in <small>, THIN SPACE; no other space comes before the next atom 508

So the spacing keeps a legarmeh with the atom before it, and puts a paseq between two atoms.

Spaces

The files write NO-BREAK SPACE and THIN SPACE as the character references &nbsp; (22,042 times) and &thinsp; (2,803 times), and have no other character reference. Each THIN SPACE is beside the PASEQ of a legarmeh or a paseq, as above. A NO-BREAK SPACE comes alone or in a run of eight:

Where Run Count
before a samekh or pe break one 3,553
after a samekh break eight 1,982
after an inverted nun one 8
before an inverted nun one 1
a space of song spacing eight 328

Song spacing, MAM-simple's shirah-space, is in these chapters, with these numbers of spaces: Exodus 15 (43), Deuteronomy 32 (67), Joshua 12 (16), Judges 5 (86), II Samuel 22 (47), Ecclesiastes 3 (27), Esther 9 (11) and I Chronicles 16 (31).

Breaks and inverted nun

Each of the 1,982 samekh breaks is {ס} in a span of class mam-spi-samekh, with a NO-BREAK SPACE before it and eight after it, and each of the 1,571 pe breaks is {פ} in a span of class mam-spi-pe, with a NO-BREAK SPACE before it and a <br> after it. Most end a verse, but 145 samekh and 24 pe breaks are inside one.

Each of the 9 inverted nun marks is ׆ (NUN HAFUKHA) in a span of class mam-spi-invnun, at Numbers 10:35–36, and Psalms 107:23–28 and 107:40.

Small, large and hung letters

A small letter is in <small> (23 times), a large letter in <big> (27 times) and a hung letter in <sup> (4 times, at Judges 18:30; Psalms 80:14; and Job 38:13 and 38:15). Each of these elements holds one letter and its marks:

Example Reference What it has
בִּשְׁפַּרְפָּרָ֖א Daniel 6:20 a small letter and a large one
רְשָׁעִ֣ים Job 38:13 a hung letter
(וגיש) [וְג֣וּשׁ] Job 7:5 a small letter in a ketiv

Ketiv and qere

Each of the 1,047 pairs of a ketiv and its qere is a span of class mam-kq, which holds the ketiv, unpointed and in parentheses, in a span of class mam-kq-k, and the qere, pointed and in square brackets, in a span of class mam-kq-q, with a separator between them: a space or, in 2 pairs, a MAQAF. The files keep the order that MAM's pages on Hebrew Wikisource have, which puts the qere first in 133 pairs, 130 of them right after a maqaf. By order, separator, and the words of each part, the pairs are of these shapes:

Example Reference Order Separator Words Count
(הוצא) [הַיְצֵ֣א] Genesis 8:17 the ketiv first a space 1, 1 887
אֶת־[יְע֥וּשׁ] (יעיש) Genesis 36:5 the qere first a space 1, 1 131
(כי טוב) [כְּט֣וֹב] Judges 16:25 the ketiv first a space 2, 1 11
(בגד) [בָּ֣א גָ֑ד] Genesis 30:11 the ketiv first a space 1, 2 8
(הייתה מוציא) [הָיִ֛יתָ הַמּוֹצִ֥יא] II Samuel 5:2 the ketiv first a space 2, 2 5
אֶת־[מֵימֵ֥י רַגְלֵיהֶ֖ם] (שניהם) II Kings 18:27 the qere first a space 1, 2 2
עַד־(יעבור)־[יַעֲבׇר־]זָֽעַם׃ Isaiah 26:20 the ketiv first a MAQAF 1, 1 1
בֶן־(בנימן)־[בָּנִ֔י מִן־]בְּנֵי־פֶ֖רֶץ I Chronicles 9:4 the ketiv first a MAQAF 1, 2 1
(תלום שם הפלשתים) [תְּלָא֥וּם שָׁ֙מָּה֙ פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים] II Samuel 21:12 the ketiv first a space 3, 3 1

A ketiv velo qere, a ketiv that is written but not read, is a span of class mam-kq-k with no pair around it, at II Samuel 13:33 and 15:21; II Kings 5:18; Jeremiah 38:16, 39:12 and 51:3; Ezekiel 48:16; and Ruth 3:12. A qere velo ketiv, a qere that is read but not written, is likewise a span of class mam-kq-q, at Judges 20:13; II Samuel 16:23 and 18:20; II Kings 19:31 and 19:37; Jeremiah 31:38 and 50:29; and Ruth 3:5 and 3:17. A trivial pair, which the guide to MAM-simple's JSON describes as a ketiv/qere “whose two forms differ in a way that needs no separate display”, is one pointed atom in a span of class mam-kq-trivial. Characters

Code points that stand for more than one mark

Some code points stand for different marks in different places: by the system of accents of the verse, prose or poetic, or, for PASEQ, by its markup. As MAM-for-Sefaria uses them:

Code point Where Count Mark
ZARQA prose verses 180 the zarqa's stress helper
ZARQA poetic verses 198 tsinnorit
ZINOR prose verses 988 zarqa
ZINOR poetic verses 251 tsinnor
PASEQ in <b> 1,787 legarmeh
PASEQ in <small> 508 paseq
YERAH BEN YOMO prose verses 16 yeraḥ ben yomo
YERAH BEN YOMO poetic verses 39 galgal
ATNAH HAFUKH poetic verses 195 atnaḥ hafukh
GERESH prose verses 4,175 geresh
GERESH MUQDAM poetic verses 2,963 geresh muqdam, which with revia is revia mugrash

ATNAH HAFUKH and GERESH MUQDAM are only in poetic verses, and GERESH only in prose verses. Each of the 2,963 atoms with a GERESH MUQDAM has it on its first letter, and also has a REVIA.

The zarqa and its stress helper

Each of the 1,239 ZINOR marks is on the last letter of its atom: the zarqa in prose verses and the tsinnor in poetic verses. Of them, 59 are on a lamed, as at Leviticus 4:2 below. In prose verses, each of the 180 ZARQA marks is the zarqa's stress helper, on an earlier letter of the atom than its ZINOR, as at Genesis 19:4:

Example Reference Code points
טֶ֘רֶם֮ Genesis 19:4 TET, SEGOL, ZARQA
RESH, SEGOL
FINAL MEM, ZINOR
יִשְׂרָאֵל֮ Leviticus 4:2 YOD, HIRIQ
SHIN, SIN DOT, SHEVA
RESH, QAMATS
ALEF, TSERE
LAMED, ZINOR

A meteg after the silluq

In 2 atoms, MAM's source identifies a silluq that has a meteg after it, on a later letter of the atom. MAM-for-Sefaria, in csv/ and csv-ajf/ alike, has the silluq and every other mark of each atom, but not that meteg, which other versions of MAM, MAM-simple among them, have:

Version I Kings 7:37 Job 4:12
Sefaria לְכֻלָּֽהְנָה מֶֽנְהוּ
other versions of MAM לְכֻלָּֽהְנָֽה מֶֽנְהֽוּ

Mark order

The marks of each letter are in MAM's order, which is not Unicode's: a SHIN DOT or SIN DOT comes first, then a DAGESH OR MAPIQ, then a RAFE, and then the other marks, in the order MAM gives them. A note in MAM-basics says more. Unicode normalization puts the marks in Unicode's order, and would change the order of the marks of 143,042 of the 306,525 atoms of csv/.

What the files leave out

The handlers of py/mb_sefaria/mam4sef_handlers.py write nothing for these three things that MAM-simple has:

  1. Its notes on scroll differences (sdt-note). The files keep the text that each note is about, and have no notes. MAM's documentation notes, which MAM-simple does not have either, are in MAM-with-doc, to which the files' Version Notes link.
  2. The verse that four books repeat after their last (good-ending).
  3. In csv/, the cant-alef and cant-bet strands of the 24 verses with two cantillations, whose text represents both strands at once. csv-ajf/ has the strands too.

Robust Unicode

Unicode normalization sorts the marks of each letter by their combining classes. A COMBINING GRAPHEME JOINER (CGJ) has combining class 0, so normalization moves no mark across one. MAM-for-Sefaria has 652 of them, each on a letter whose marks normalization would otherwise put in another order: it keeps the vowel or METEG after it in place after the marks before it. Every letter of the files that has two vowels has a CGJ between them. The tables give, for each kind, the code points of the letter in order, and the order that normalization would give them without the CGJ.

Jerusalem

638 are in atoms spelled ירושלם (634) or ירושלמה (4), with or without a prefix, on the lamed. It has its own vowel, PATAH or QAMATS, then, in all but 1 of them, an accent or METEG, and after the CGJ an orphaned HIRIQ or SHEVA, the vowel of the yod that the spelling lacks:

Example Reference The lamed's code points Normalized without the CGJ Count

יְרוּשָׁלָ֑͏ִם Joshua 15:8 LAMED, QAMATS, ETNAHTA, CGJ, HIRIQ LAMED, HIRIQ, QAMATS, ETNAHTA 286

Two strands on one letter

The other 14 are in verses with two cantillations, on a letter whose text represents both strands: the marks before the CGJ are one strand's, and the marks after it are the other's. csv-ajf/ has the strands too, with no CGJ on that letter, which the tables show in the attention color. They give each atom's references in both folders, since the two numberings differ in the Decalogues. In 4 atoms, one strand has a QAMATS and an accent or METEG below the letter, and the other a PATAH and an accent above it:
